{{short description|Type of Abelian category (in category theory in mathematics)}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Grothendieck category''' is a certain kind of [[abelian category]], introduced in [[Alexander Grothendieck]]'s [[Grothendieck's Tôhoku paper|Tôhoku paper of 1957]]<ref name="tohoku">{{citation|first=Alexander|last=Grothendieck|author-link=Alexander Grothendieck|title=Sur quelques points d'algèbre homologique|journal=[[Tôhoku Mathematical Journal]]|volume=9|issue=2|series=(2)|pages=119–221|year=1957|mr=0102537|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.tmj/1178244839|doi=10.2748/tmj/1178244839|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}. [http://www.math.mcgill.ca/barr/papers/gk.pdf English translation].</ref> in order to develop the machinery of [[homological algebra]] for [[module (mathematics)|module]]s and for [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]] in a unified manner. The theory of these categories was further developed in [[Pierre Gabriel]]'s 1962 thesis.<ref name="gabriel-these">{{citation|first=Pierre|last=Gabriel|author-link=Pierre Gabriel|title=Des catégories abéliennes|url=http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~aar/papers/gabriel.pdf|journal=Bull. Soc. Math. Fr.|volume=90|pages=323–448|year=1962|doi=10.24033/bsmf.1583|doi-access=free}}</ref>

To every [[algebraic variety]] <math>V</math> one can associate a Grothendieck category <math>\operatorname{Qcoh}(V)</math>, consisting of the [[quasi-coherent sheaf|quasi-coherent sheaves]] on <math>V</math>. This category encodes all the relevant geometric information about <math>V</math>, and <math>V</math> can be recovered from <math>\operatorname{Qcoh}(V)</math> (the [[Gabriel–Rosenberg reconstruction theorem]]). This example gives rise to one approach to [[noncommutative algebraic geometry]]: the study of "non-commutative varieties" is then nothing but the study of (certain) Grothendieck categories.<ref>{{citation|author1-first=Hoang Dinh|author1-last=Van|author2-first=Liyu|author2-last=Liu|author3-first=Wendy|author3-last=Lowen|title=Non-commutative deformations and quasi-coherent modules|journal=Selecta Mathematica|volume=23|pages=1061-1119|year=2016|mr=3624905|arxiv=1411.0331|doi=10.1007/s00029-016-0263-9}}</ref>

==Definition==
By definition, a Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is an [[AB5 category]] with a [[Generator (category theory)|generator]]. Spelled out, this means that
* <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is an [[abelian category]];
* every (possibly infinite) family of objects in <math>\mathcal{A}</math> has a [[coproduct]] (also known as direct sum) in <math>\mathcal{A}</math>;
* [[direct limit]]s of [[short exact sequence]]s are exact; this means that if a direct system of [[short exact sequence]]s in <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is given, then the induced sequence of direct limits is a short exact sequence as well. (Direct limits are always [[exact functor|right-exact]]; the important point here is that we require them to be [[exact functor|left-exact]] as well.)
* <math>\mathcal{A}</math> possesses a generator, i.e. there is an object <math>G</math> in <math>\mathcal{A}</math> such that <math>\operatorname{Hom}(G,-)</math> is a [[faithful functor]] from <math>\mathcal{A}</math> to the [[category of sets]]. (In our situation, this is equivalent to saying that every object <math>X</math> of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> admits an [[epimorphism]] <math>G^{(I)}\rightarrow X</math>, where <math>G^{(I)}</math> denotes a direct sum of copies of <math>G</math>, one for each element of the (possibly infinite) set <math>I</math>.)

The name "Grothendieck category" appeared neither in Grothendieck's Tôhoku paper<ref name="tohoku"/> nor in Gabriel's thesis;<ref name="gabriel-these"/> it came into use in the second half of the 1960s in the work of several authors, including Jan-Erik Roos, Bo Stenström, Ulrich Oberst, and Bodo Pareigis. (Some authors use a different definition, not requiring the existence of a generator.)

==Examples==
* The prototypical example of a Grothendieck category is the [[category of abelian groups]]; the abelian group <math>\Z</math> of integers is a generator.
* More generally, given any [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>R</math> (associative, with <math>1</math>, but not necessarily commutative), the category <math>\operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> of all right (or alternatively: left) [[module (mathematics)|module]]s over <math>R</math> is a Grothendieck category; <math>R</math> itself is a generator.
* Given a [[topological space]] <math>X</math>, the category of all [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]] of abelian groups on <math>X</math> is a Grothendieck category.<ref name="tohoku"/> (More generally: the category of all sheaves of right <math>R</math>-modules on <math>X</math> is a Grothendieck category for any ring <math>R</math>.)  
* Given a [[ringed space]] <math>(X,\mathcal{O}_X)</math>, the category of [[Sheaves of modules|sheaves of ''O<sub>X</sub>''-modules]] is a Grothendieck category.<ref name="tohoku"/>
* Given an (affine or projective) [[algebraic variety]] <math>V</math> (or more generally: any [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] or [[algebraic stack]]), the category <math>\operatorname{Qcoh}(V)</math> of [[quasi-coherent sheaf|quasi-coherent sheaves]] on <math>V</math> is a Grothendieck category.<ref>{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 077P | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/077P}}; {{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0781 | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0781}}.</ref>
* Given a small site (''C'', ''J'') (i.e. a small category ''C'' together with a [[Grothendieck topology]] ''J''), the category of all sheaves of abelian groups on the site is a Grothendieck category.

=== Constructing further Grothendieck categories ===

* Any category that's [[equivalence of categories|equivalent]] to a Grothendieck category is itself a Grothendieck category.
* Given Grothendieck categories  <math>\mathcal{A_1},\ldots,\mathcal{A_n}</math>, the [[product category]]  <math>\mathcal{A_1}\times\ldots\times\mathcal{A_n}</math> is a Grothendieck category.
* Given a [[Category (mathematics)#Small and large categories|small category]] <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and a Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, the [[functor category]] <math>\operatorname{Funct}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})</math>, consisting of all [[covariant functor]]s from <math>\mathcal{C}</math> to <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, is a Grothendieck category.<ref name="tohoku" />
* Given a small [[preadditive category|preadditive]] category <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and a Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, the functor category <math>\operatorname{Add}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})</math> of all additive covariant functors from <math>\mathcal{C}</math> to <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is a Grothendieck category.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vsfyCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA487|title=Algebra: Rings, Modules and Categories I|last=Faith|first=Carl|publisher=Springer|year=1973|pages=486–498|language=en|isbn=9783642806346}}</ref>
* If <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is a Grothendieck category and <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is a [[localizing subcategory]] of <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, then both <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and the [[Serre quotient category]] <math>\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{C}</math> are Grothendieck categories.<ref name="gabriel-these" />

==Properties and theorems==
Every Grothendieck category contains an [[injective cogenerator]]. For example, an injective cogenerator of the category of abelian groups is the [[quotient group]] <math>\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}</math>.

Every object in a Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> has an [[injective hull]] in <math>\mathcal{A}</math>.<ref name="tohoku"/><ref name="gabriel-these"/>  This allows to construct [[injective resolution]]s and thereby the use of the tools of [[homological algebra]] in <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, in order to define [[derived functor]]s. (Note that not all Grothendieck categories allow [[projective resolution]]s for all objects; examples are categories of sheaves of abelian groups on many topological spaces, such as on the space of real numbers.)

In a Grothendieck category, any family of [[subobject]]s <math>(U_i)</math> of a given object <math>X</math> has a [[supremum]] (or "sum") <math display="inline">\sum_i U_i</math> as well as an [[infimum]] (or "intersection") <math>\cap_i U_i</math>, both of which are again subobjects of <math>X</math>. Further, if the family <math>(U_i)</math> is directed (i.e. for any two objects in the family, there is a third object in the family that contains the two), and <math>V</math> is another subobject of <math>X</math>, we have<ref>Stenström, Prop. V.1.1</ref>

:<math>\sum_{i}(U_i\cap V) = \left(\sum_{i}U_i\right) \cap V.</math>

Grothendieck categories are [[Subobject|well-powered]] (sometimes called ''locally small'', although that term is also used for a different concept), i.e. the collection of subobjects of any given object forms a set (rather than a [[proper class]]).<ref name=":0" />

It is a rather deep result that every Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is [[Complete category|complete]],<ref>Stenström, Cor. X.4.4</ref> i.e. that arbitrary [[limit (category theory)|limit]]s (and in particular [[product (category theory)|product]]s) exist in <math>\mathcal{A}</math>. By contrast, it follows directly from the definition that <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is co-complete, i.e. that arbitrary [[limit (category theory)|colimits]] and [[coproduct]]s (direct sums) exist in <math>\mathcal{A}</math>. Coproducts in a Grothendieck category are exact (i.e. the coproduct of a family of short exact sequences is again a short exact sequence), but products need not be exact.

A functor <math>F \colon {\cal A} \to {\cal X}</math> from a Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> to an arbitrary category <math>\mathcal{X}</math> has a [[Adjoint functors|left adjoint]] if and only if it commutes with all limits, and it has a right adjoint if and only if it commutes with all colimits. This follows from [[Peter J. Freyd]]'s ''special adjoint functor theorem'' and its dual.<ref>{{Cite book|title=[[Categories for the Working Mathematician]]|edition=2nd|last=Mac Lane| first=Saunders|author-link=Saunders Mac Lane| publisher=Springer|year=1978|pages=130|language=en}}</ref>

The [[Gabriel–Popescu theorem]] states that any Grothendieck category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is equivalent to a [[full subcategory]] of the category <math>\operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> of right modules over some unital ring <math>R</math> (which can be taken to be the [[endomorphism ring]] of a generator of <math>\mathcal{A}</math>), and <math>\mathcal{A}</math> can be obtained as a [[Quotient of an abelian category|Gabriel quotient]] of <math>\operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> by some [[localizing subcategory]].<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Nicolae| last1=Popescu|author1-link=Nicolae Popescu|first2= Pierre| last2=Gabriel|author2-link=Pierre Gabriel|title=Caractérisation des catégories abéliennes avec générateurs et limites inductives exactes|journal=[[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences]]|volume=258|year=1964|pages=4188–4190}}</ref>

As a consequence of Gabriel–Popescu, one can show that every Grothendieck category is [[locally presentable category|locally presentable]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Šťovíček|first=Jan|date=2013-01-01|title=Deconstructibility and the Hill Lemma in Grothendieck categories|journal=Forum Mathematicum|language=en|volume=25|issue=1|arxiv=1005.3251|bibcode=2010arXiv1005.3251S|doi=10.1515/FORM.2011.113|s2cid=119129714}}</ref> Furthermore, Gabriel-Popescu can be used to see that every Grothendieck category is complete, being a [[reflective subcategory]] of the complete category <math>\operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> for some <math>R</math>. 

Every small abelian category <math>\mathcal{C}</math> can be embedded in a Grothendieck category, in the following fashion. The category <math>\mathcal{A}:=\operatorname{Lex}(\mathcal{C}^{op},\mathrm{Ab})</math> of [[Exact functor|left-exact]] additive (covariant) functors <math>\mathcal{C}^{op}\rightarrow\mathrm{Ab}</math> (where <math>\mathrm{Ab}</math> denotes the [[category of abelian groups]]) is a Grothendieck category, and the functor <math>h\colon\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}</math>, with <math>C\mapsto h_C=\operatorname{Hom}(-,C)</math>, is full, faithful and exact. A generator of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is given by the coproduct of all <math>h_C</math>, with <math>C\in\mathcal{C}</math>.<ref name="gabriel-these" /> The category <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is equivalent to the category <math>\text{Ind}(\mathcal C)</math> of [[Filtered category|ind-objects]] of <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and the embedding <math>h</math> corresponds to the natural embedding  <math>\mathcal{C}\to\text{Ind}(\mathcal C)</math>. We may therefore view <math>\mathcal{A}</math> as the co-completion of <math>\mathcal{C}</math>.

=== Special kinds of objects and Grothendieck categories ===
An object <math>X</math> in a Grothendieck category is called ''finitely generated'' if, whenever <math>X</math> is written as the sum of a family of subobjects of <math>X</math>, then it is already the sum of a finite subfamily. (In the case <math>{\cal A} = \operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> of module categories, this notion is equivalent to the familiar notion of [[finitely generated module]]s.) Epimorphic images of finitely generated objects are again finitely generated. If <math>U\subseteq X</math> and both <math>U</math> and <math>X/U</math> are finitely generated, then so is <math>X</math>. The object <math>X</math> is finitely generated if, and only if, for any directed system <math>(A_i)</math> in <math>{\cal A}</math> in which each morphism is a monomorphism, the natural morphism <math>\varinjlim \mathrm{Hom}(X,A_i)\to \mathrm{Hom}(X,\varinjlim A_i)</math> is an isomorphism.<ref>Stenström, Prop. V.3.2</ref> A Grothendieck category need not contain any non-zero finitely generated objects. 

A Grothendieck category is called ''locally finitely generated'' if it has a set of finitely generated generators (i.e. if there exists a family <math>(G_i)_{i\in I}</math> of finitely generated objects such that to every object <math>X</math> there exist <math>i\in I</math> and a non-zero morphism <math>G_{i}\rightarrow X</math>; equivalently: <math>X</math> is epimorphic image of a direct sum of copies of the <math>G_{i}</math>). In such a category, every object is the sum of its finitely generated subobjects.<ref name=":0" /> Every category <math>{\cal A} = \operatorname{Mod}(R)</math> is locally finitely generated.

An object <math>X</math> in a Grothendieck category is called ''finitely presented'' if it is finitely generated and if every epimorphism <math>W\to X</math> with finitely generated domain <math>W</math> has a finitely generated kernel. Again, this generalizes the notion of [[finitely presented module]]s.  If <math>U\subseteq X</math> and both <math>U</math> and <math>X/U</math> are finitely presented, then so is <math>X</math>.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}}  In a locally finitely generated Grothendieck category <math>{\cal A}</math>, the finitely presented objects can be characterized as follows:<ref>Stenström, Prop. V.3.4</ref> <math>X</math> in <math>{\cal A}</math> is finitely presented if, and only if, for every directed system <math>(A_i)</math> in <math>{\cal A}</math>, the natural morphism <math>\varinjlim \mathrm{Hom}(X,A_i)\to \mathrm{Hom}(X,\varinjlim A_i)</math> is an isomorphism.

A Grothendieck category is ''locally finitely presented'' if it has a set of finitely presented generators, which is equivalent to saying that every object is a direct limit of finitely presented objects.

An object <math>X</math> in a Grothendieck category <math>{\cal A}</math> is called ''coherent'' if it is finitely presented and if each of its finitely generated subobjects is also finitely presented.<ref name="herzog">{{Cite journal|last=Herzog|first=I.|date=1997|title=The Ziegler Spectrum of a Locally Coherent Grothendieck Category|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/231890405|journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=74|issue=3|pages=503–558|doi=10.1112/S002461159700018X|s2cid=121827768 }}</ref> (This generalizes the notion of [[Coherent sheaf|coherent sheaves]] on a ringed space.) The full subcategory of all coherent objects in <math>{\cal A}</math> is abelian and the inclusion functor is [[exact functor|exact]].<ref name="herzog" />

An object <math>X</math> in a Grothendieck category is called ''[[Noetherian]]'' if the set of its subobjects satisfies the [[ascending chain condition]], i.e. if every sequence <math>X_1\subseteq X_2 \subseteq \cdots</math> of subobjects of <math>X</math> eventually becomes stationary. This is the case if and only if every subobject of X is finitely generated. (In the case <math>{\cal A} = \operatorname{Mod}(R)</math>, this notion is equivalent to the familiar notion of [[Noetherian module|Noetherian modules]].) A Grothendieck category is called ''locally Noetherian'' if it has a set of Noetherian generators; an example is the category of left modules over a left-[[Noetherian ring]].

A Grothendieck category is called ''spectral'' if every short exact sequence [[Split exact sequence|splits]]. To a given Grothendieck category <math>{\cal A}</math> one can define a spectral Grothendieck category <math>\operatorname{Spec} {\cal A}</math> and a canonical functor <math>P : {\cal A} \to \operatorname{Spec} {\cal A}</math>. The objects of <math>\operatorname{Spec} {\cal A}</math> correspond, up to isomorphism, to the injective objects of <math>{\cal A}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gabriel |first=Peter |last2=Oberst |first2=Ulrich |date=1966-10-01 |title=Spektralkategorien und reguläre Ringe in Von-Neumannschen Sinn |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01112218 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |language=de |volume=92 |issue=5 |pages=389–395 |doi=10.1007/BF01112218 |issn=1432-1823|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The functor <math>P
</math> turns all [[Essential monomorphism|essential monomorphisms]] into isomorphisms and thus identifies each object of <math>{\cal A}</math> with its injective hull. This allows to define useful dimension-like functions on <math>{\cal A}</math>: for each indecomposable injective object <math>I</math> in <math>{\cal A}</math> and every object <math>A</math> in <math>{\cal A}</math>, the [[cardinal number]] <math>r_I(A)</math> measures, roughly speaking, how many direct summands isomorphic to ''<math>I</math>'' appear in the injective hull of <math>A</math>.
